messages.content:
You are evaluating a PTSD case vignette for the presence of causal
connections between five Ehlers & Clark cognitive components: Triggers, Negative Appraisals, Memory,
Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies.

For each of the 20 ordered, directed (A -> B) pairs of distinct components, decide whether the
vignette conveys, in some paragraph, that A influences, drives, or leads to B. Apply the same
causal standard as a structural validator:

COMPONENT SYNONYMS (any of these synonyms count as the component appearing):
  Triggers              -> "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals   -> "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory                -> "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat                -> "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies-> "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "safety behaviours", "maladaptive coping"

CAUSAL STANDARD
An edge A -> B is PRESENT (return 1) iff, within the same paragraph:
  (i) both A and B (or their synonyms) appear; AND
  (ii) the paragraph conveys that A influences / drives / leads to B, through direct causal
       language, sequential structure, or connecting phrases like "because of", "this meant",
       "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
If no paragraph conveys the A -> B relationship, return 0 for that edge.

You will return a binary judgement for each of the 20 ordered pairs. Be strict: do not assume
an edge based on mere co-occurrence; the paragraph must actually convey directional influence.

Evaluate the following vignette and judge each of the 20 directed edges
(A -> B) on whether the vignette conveys A influencing B.

VIGNETTE
Mateo was fifty-four when the accumulation of unspoken moments finally required him to step into a therapist's office. He had been forty-two when a routine welfare check turned into a warrant service that shattered his daily rhythm. Officers breached the apartment door without warning, moving with practiced speed. When Mateo reached for his badge to identify himself, a rifle shifted toward his chest. Hands pinned him to the concrete, knees driving into his back, the smell of dust and sweat thick in the air. A shouted command cut through the ringing in his ears, followed by the cold bite of cuffs. The violence was sudden, absolute, and entirely unprovoked by any resistance on his part. When he was finally released, the case was closed with no internal review, no apology, just a file stamped unfounded complaint. He walked out of the precinct with his uniform intact but his sense of safety gone. In the months that followed, Mateo found himself unable to hold the full account in his mind. Whenever the scene tried to surface, he would close his eyes and deliberately look away, pushing the image of the concrete floor and the weight of the rifles out of his focus. The memory felt like a photograph left too long in the sun, faded at the edges, impossible to verify. He would tell his wife, Elena, that it had been terrible, but when she asked what actually happened, he would trail off. He knew pieces of it, the sound of the door, the pressure on his shoulders, but the rest was gone, swallowed by a gap he could not cross. The story felt too extreme to be real, a detail so sharp it made him doubt his own mind. He navigated his days as a parole officer carrying these gaps, the constant outward sweep of his eyes, the sudden jumps at ordinary sounds, and the familiar tightening of betrayal and injustice. He walked through the precinct and the neighborhoods he covered tracking exits, noting who stood too still, watching hands. He was certain that stillness was the precursor to movement, that a sudden quiet in the hallway meant something dangerous was being prepared. He jumped at the clatter of files, at the sharp knock of a door, his body bracing before his mind could catch up. His cruiser parked outside every parolee's home, the dashboard heavy with case files and radio static. When he saw people misbehave in the hallway, or when voices in the waiting room climbed into arguments, Mateo's heart would begin to pound against his ribs. He would grip the edge of his desk until the rhythm slowed, aware that the stress of the moment was pulling him back to that cold floor. The unprovoked force he had endured made every quiet room feel charged, every sudden shift in posture a potential escalation, which is why the sight of disorder and the hum of stress now registered as immediate danger. He carried the belief that the very people tasked with upholding order had turned on him without consequence, that the system had protected its own while leaving him to carry the weight of what happened. He stopped attending the department's wellness seminars, telling Elena he had too much paperwork. He began routing his afternoon visits through back alleys, avoiding the main precinct courtyard where colleagues gathered for debriefs. The distance between him and his team grew quiet and formal. He stopped discussing the cases that felt too heavy, and Elena noticed how he would sit at the kitchen table long after dinner, staring at the wall, his hands resting lightly on the wood as if waiting for something to happen. She watched him pack his bag each evening, the same bag that held his badge, his notes, and the unspoken weight of a system he no longer trusted. She noticed how he would pause at the threshold of the front door, listening to the house fall still, his shoulders rising as if bracing against a blow that had already passed. The gaps in his memory and the sharp appraisals of unfairness sat side by side, heavy but unlinked, occupying the same quiet space. The turning point came last month when a routine intake went silent. The parolee sat perfectly still, eyes down, and Mateo felt his pulse hammer in his throat, a frantic rhythm that left him breathless. He couldn't finish the session. He sat in his car in the precinct lot, gripping the steering wheel, certain that he was losing his footing. He had come to see Elena and ask for help, not because he knew what to do, but because the weight of carrying it alone was becoming heavier than he could manage. He hoped someone might help him make sense of the silence, the jumping nerves, the gaps in his own mind, and he feared that if he didn't speak to a professional soon, he would never trust his own perception again.

output.rationale: Triggers cause threat (sounds cause bracing), memory causes negative appraisals (gaps cause doubt), memory causes threat (event makes rooms charged), memory causes maladaptive strategies (intrusion leads to avoidance), threat causes negative appraisals (symptoms lead to self-doubt), threat causes memory (stress pulls to memory), threat causes maladaptive strategies (heart pounding leads to gripping), and negative appraisals cause maladaptive strategies (belief leads to avoidance).
